source.title: Repurposing Language Models into Embedding Models: Finding the Compute-Optimal Recipe
source.authors: M. Jamnik; Albert Qiaochu Jiang; Wen-Da Li; Piotr Milos; Bartosz Piotrowski; Alicja Ziarko

record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law experiments to contrastive fine-tuning of decoder-only language models into text embedding models, rather than testing held-out next-token pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study reports contrastive fine-tuning losses, fitted loss relationships, compute-budget trends, predictions on held-out or different-family models, and downstream MTEB results. These are embedding fine-tuning outcomes, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy. The per-run loss points in many plots have no numerical values in the text.
record.test_reason: The study fits power-law-style laws to contrastive fine-tuning loss of pretrained Pythia models over three orders of magnitude of compute. It predicts a held-out larger model and another model family, and relates loss to MTEB scores. This is a new training regime (V5) with partial bearing on V2, V3, V6 and V7. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss (V1) or vary shape at fixed size (V4).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that contrastive fine-tuning of decoder-only LMs follows fittable scaling laws, using a modified Chinchilla formula with a trainable-fraction term. This yields a recipe: full fine-tuning below about 9.06e16 FLOP and LoRA above, with model size read from IsoFLOP-derived lookups. They conjecture, without testing, that the formula extends to larger scales. They show prediction on a 2x larger Pythia model and on two Gemma 2B-class models. They acknowledge single-seed runs, one model family, one readout, and a partial MTEB evaluation.
record.recipe_differences: The study concerns contrastive embedding fine-tuning rather than next-token pretraining. It fits a formula that includes trainable-parameter fraction, compares several fine-tuning methods, and chooses model size, data quantity, and method for a compute budget.
record.method_sensitivity: Fine-tuning method changes achievable loss and the fitted loss-versus-budget slope; full fine-tuning and LoRA have reported slopes −0.21 and −0.22. The modified formula includes trainable-parameter fraction. The paper also reports robustness of its formula to batch size 2048 and context length 512, compared with the main setup of batch size 1024 and context length 75.

fits_no_version.finding: The compute-optimal fine-tuning method switches: full fine-tuning is best below 9.06e16 FLOP and LoRA above. LoRA ranks 32–128 are optimal, and freezing 50–70% of blocks is optimal for about 1B-parameter models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The compute-optimal parameter-efficient fine-tuning method and its hyperparameters shift with compute budget.

record.problems: Each experiment was run exactly once, with no averaging over random seeds; the paper notes this may leave noisy conclusions. Error bars and statistical significance tests for the main experimental results are not reported. The main loss is contrastive training loss rather than held-out pretraining loss. Most loss and downstream plots do not provide numerical values in the text, and downstream evaluation uses a representative MTEB subset rather than the full benchmark.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported figure-only loss datapoints for each Pythia size, compute budget, block-freezing fraction, or LoRA rank were extracted; those grids are plotted across Figures 2–5 and 18–22, with many combinations and no textual numerical values. Individual MTEB task/model datapoints were not extracted from Figures 8–11.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy versus N, D or C is not measured; only contrastive fine-tuning loss of already-pretrained models.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude: the held-out model is only about 2x the largest fit model.
Stable power-law exponents for optimal N and optimal D versus compute, and the Kaplan-vs-Chinchilla split.
Depth/width at fixed parameter count is not varied.
Other modalities, repeated-data regimes, and fine-tuning objectives other than contrastive embedding training.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss.
Parameter counting, schedule, or data choices for pretraining laws; disagreement between published laws.

missing.what: A formula fit on batch 1024 / context 75 predicts losses at batch 2048 / context 512 (Pythia 14M–410M, up to 9.6e16 FLOP). It is described as very good, with no numbers.

Loss vs FLOP per model size is approximately linear on log-log axes only when severely constrained budgets are excluded. Full fine-tuning IsoFLOP profiles are flatter when size and budget are both small or both large. These are bends from a single power law.
In the data-constrained view (loss vs tokens), the largest model gives the best loss at a fixed token count.

record.verdict_notes: All losses are in-training contrastive losses of pretrained models, so the study bears on V5 (fine-tuning regime), not on V1. The Gemma tests are cross-family checks at a similar scale and were unlinked from V2. Pythia models are overtrained to different degrees, which the authors flag as possibly affecting optimal size vs budget. Most quantitative results are figure-only, and no error metrics are given for the prediction claims.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures contrastive fine-tuning loss, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction is tested on Pythia 2.8B and Gemma models, but the text does not establish predictions across runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitting runs.

The study examines compute-optimal model sizes for embedding fine-tuning and provides a recipe for data quantity, but does not report a stable power-law fit for both optimal parameter count and optimal token count against compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count is reported.
Tests contrastive embedding fine-tuning of text models only; other modalities, repeated-data regimes, and other transfer or fine-tuning objectives are not tested.
Downstream evaluation uses a representative subset of MTEB; the study does not test downstream performance as a function of held-out pretraining loss.

The study compares fitting formulas and fine-tuning methods in its embedding setting, but does not test whether the original pretraining laws disagree across parameter-counting, training-schedule, or data choices, nor whether pretraining curves bend away from power laws.

rows.subject: Pythia suite
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained on the Pile for 300 billion tokens; contrastively fine-tuned into embedding models
rows.operation_detail: Fit the modified loss formula over model size, training tokens, and trainable-parameter fraction.
rows.measure: Contrastive fine-tuning loss as a function of model parameters and training tokens; the paper says the modified formula describes the observed behavior reasonably well.
rows.value: L(S, N, D) = C + (ad · log(D) + bd)/N^α + (as · (1 − S)^bs + cs)/D^β
rows.note: This is a fitted embedding fine-tuning loss formula, not a held-out pretraining cross-entropy law. Fitted coefficient values are not stated here.
rows.check: The study fits the Chinchilla form ('reasonably describes'), but a modified formula with a trainable fraction S and a log(D) term fits better. Formula comparison belongs to r17, so V7 is removed here. The value gives the formula, not fitted coefficients.
